title: Move Over, T. rex — There's a New King in Town, and It Swam!
summary: Imagine a sea monster as long as a school bus, with a mouth full of teeth like steak knives. That's Tylosaurus rex — the 'king of the knob lizards'! Scientists just discovered this ancient ocean predator, and it ruled the seas 80 million years ago. That's 13 million years before T. rex stomped on land. Its fossils were hiding in museums for decades, but everyone thought they were a smaller cousin. Then, two sharp-eyed paleontologists noticed something was different. Dr. Michael Polcyn saw a weird fossil in Texas. Years later, Dr. Amelia Zietlow spotted another odd one in New York. They checked dozens of fossils and found the truth: these were a brand-new species! The biggest clue? The teeth. Tylosaurus rex had sharp, jagged teeth for slicing prey, while its cousin had smooth, cone-shaped teeth for grabbing. Also, the new king was found mostly in Texas, while the cousin lived in Kansas. The coolest fossil is 'The Black Knight' — a giant skeleton found near Dallas in 1979. It has a broken jaw that healed, proving this beast was tough enough to survive and keep hunting. So next time you think of ancient monsters, remember: the ocean had its own T. rex, and it was just as scary!
why_it_matters: This discovery shows that even old museum collections can hold secrets — if you stay curious and observe carefully, you might discover something amazing too.

background_read: Most people think of dinosaurs like T. rex when they hear 'fossils', but many giant reptiles lived in the oceans too.
These sea creatures, called mosasaurs, were the top predators of their time, ruling warm shallow seas that covered parts of North America.
Paleontologists sometimes find fossils in museums that were mislabeled for years, waiting for someone to look more closely.
Article_Structure: WHO: Two paleontologists, Dr. Michael Polcyn and Dr. Amelia Zietlow.
WHAT: They discovered Tylosaurus rex, a new giant ocean predator as long as a school bus.
WHERE: Mainly in Texas (USA), with a cousin species living in Kansas.
WHY: The fossils were thought to be a smaller cousin until the scientists noticed the jagged teeth and the pattern of being found in Texas.

perspectives.description: Finding a new top predator shows how much is still unknown about ancient oceans and fills in a missing piece of the dinosaur-age puzzle.
Some scientists might want more evidence before agreeing it truly is a separate species, since differences in teeth can sometimes be variations within one species.
The story highlights how important it is to re-examine old fossils in museums — treasures can hide in plain sight for decades.
